_comment: LOCAL RUNTIME STATE -- two gitignored files under .fux/runtime/ that this
Both shipped in W-82 with their shapes described ONLY in a docstring, and
both readers hand-rolled defensive parsing field by field: an `_int_or_none`
helper here, an `isinstance` filter there. That is five lines of per-field
suspicion in each file, which is exactly the drift a declaration removes --
add a field and you must remember to teach the reader about it, or it is
silently dropped on the next read.
THE DEFENSIVENESS IS NOT PARANOIA AND MUST SURVIVE. These files can be
truncated by a killed process, hand-edited by someone debugging a failing
URL, or written by an older fux. `schema.coerce` is what replaces the
hand-rolled version: it keeps declared, well-typed fields and drops the
rest, so a corrupt file degrades to 'what we can still believe' rather than

_doc: One URL's entry in `url-state.json`.
COUNTED IN RUNS, NEVER IN SECONDS, and that is a law rather than a
preference: `refer/fetchcache.py` states that wall clock lives in the TTL
store and nowhere else, which ADR-REFER rests on. W-75 had specified this
file with `validated_at` and `changed_at` -- two timestamps -- and
shipping them would have been a quiet contradiction of an accepted
record.
`token` is DELIBERATELY ABSENT. It belongs to the optional `validate()`
fetcher function, which is an unruled fork gated on a measurement.
Declaring a field nothing writes is how a knob that cannot work ships.

last_seen_run.doc: run_seq of the last run whose fetch succeeded; absent = never

last_changed_run.doc: run_seq when the sanitized sha last actually moved

fail_streak.doc: consecutive failed fetches; any success resets it

run_seq.doc: networked runs so far; only a run that FETCHED increments it

urls.doc: url -> url_health, and a de-listed url is dropped entirely

rate_limited.doc: host -> how many times that host rate-limited a fetch. COUNTS, NOT CLOCKS, like every other field here (W-82 ruling 12). Keyed by HOST rather than URL because a rate limit is a property of the server, not of one page; `fux doctor` reports it so a consumer can lower `[sources.url] max_parallel` themselves. **Fux never changes the cap on their behalf** -- state the cost, do not clamp the knob

_doc: The whole of `url-shas.json` -- the sha each URL last produced.
It exists so `last_changed_run` can mean something. Without it, 'we
fetched it' and 'it changed' are indistinguishable, and a URL fetched
daily and never edited would look like it changes daily.
Kept beside the health file rather than read out of the committed index:
by the time it is consulted the new record has not been written yet, so
reading the index would compare a value with itself.
The whole of `last-cited.json` -- what the previous answer to each
question cited.
A REPORT, NOT A MEMO, and the shape is the proof: only `(loc, sha)` pairs
are stored, never an answer. `answer --memo` was proposed and withdrawn,
and its sharpest hazard was that a memo validated by a TTL hit would
replay an answer on bytes nobody confirmed while reporting `current`.
There is nothing here to replay.
The KEY is a truncated hash of the whitespace-normalised, lowercased
question -- so a repeat with different spacing is the same question, and
the user's query text never lands in a file that sits in a shared
checkout's working tree.
